summary: The note analyzes expected effects on employment of the September 15, 2023 decision to raise the federal minimum wage to $15 an hour by 2025. It covers reactions from small and large businesses, automation, the gig economy, youth and unskilled workers, sector and geographic differences, and the role of education and workforce development. Experts predict short-term disruption, accelerated automation, and a need for retraining.
one_line: Analysis of how the federal minimum wage rise to $15 by 2025 may reshape employment, automation, gig work, youth jobs, and workforce education.
key_facts: On September 15, 2023, a decision was made to raise the federal minimum wage to $15 an hour by 2025.
The increase was backed by labor unions and social justice organizations and championed by Senator John Keen and Congresswoman Linda Martes.
Sarah Cho, who owns a bakery in Centerville, is exploring automation, staff training, and price adjustments to keep margins without laying off employees.
SuperSave Retail, led by CEO Richard Hanson, publicly welcomed the hike, though analysts speculate it may increase part-time and temporary positions to offset labor costs.
A November 12, 2023 study by the Economic and Labor Research Institute (ELRI) suggests higher labor costs may accelerate automation in food service, manufacturing, and retail.
Dr. Emily Tran of the University of New Workings said blue-collar jobs' viability will rely on workers' ability to complement, rather than compete with, technology.
Tomás Herrera, a gig economy researcher, spoke at a December 5, 2023 seminar about the wage rise driving more people into gig work and the need to reevaluate protections for gig workers.
Margaret Singh of the Market Workforce Advisory predicts a short-term contraction in youth employment opportunities but a long-term expansion as labor markets stabilize.
The fast-food industry may be heavily affected by automation, while caregiving, which relies on human interaction, may see fewer changes and possibly greater demand, per James Allen's experience.
Urban areas with higher living costs may absorb wage increases more easily than rural areas, where small businesses have tighter margins.
Academics broadly agree that STEAM education will be important for preparing future workers.
Midtown Technical Institute, led by Chancellor Rebecca Flores, is adapting its curriculum to teach 'cross-functional skills that meet the demands of a technologically enriched workplace.'
